newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Shell builds US Gulf deepwater portfolio.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Shell builds US Gulf deepwater portfolio.

text.p: Shell Offshore Inc this week acquired lease rights on thousands of acres off the coast of Texas, adding to its portfolio of deepwater prospects in the Gulf of Mexico.
The tracts, included one lying under more than 10,000 feet of water, hold the promise of huge reservoirs of crude oil and natural gas, said Mark Leonard, deepwater prospect manager.
"The structures out there are pretty big," the Shell Offshore executive said, "(but) there isn't a well to give us an idea of exactly what's out there."

Shell Offshore, an affiliate of Houston-based Shell Oil Co, was the most aggressive bidder in the record-setting western Gulf lease sale this week, spending a total $62 million to place winning bids on 123 blocks.
The lease sale drew a record 929 bids and $356.1 million in high bids, with interest in deepwater tracts fueled by lower royalty rates designed to boost domestic oil production.

In a consortium with Texaco Inc and Amoco Corp, Shell Offshore won rights to the deepest tract in the lease round, a section of the Alaminos Canyon lying in more than 10,000 feet of water 156 miles from Port Isabel, Texas.

That prospect lies well out of the reach of modern drilling technology, and probably will not be explored before the turn of the century unless there are revolutionary advances in drilling technology, he said.
Shell Offshore in April spudded the deepest well so far in the Gulf, drilling its first Baha well in 7,620 feet of water in Alaminos Canyon, which lies 150 miles off the Texas coast.

But that well, drilled into a rise in the sea bed elevated by what is believed to be a hydrocarbon-bearing structure below, was not completed because of an undisclosed mechanical failure, Leonard said.
"We're going to go back to the drawing board on that one," he said. Additional seismic surveys are planned but a drilling schedule has not been set, he said.

Despite the failed attempt to complete its Baha well, Shell Offshore was so anxious to win lease rights in the Alaminos Canyon area that it three times outbid its own consortium to win drilling rights on nearby blocks.

In sealed bids, Shell put down a total $6.9 million on three contiguous blocks in the offshore canyon, each time upping what would have been a winning bid from the consortium formed with Amoco and Texaco.
"Shell placed a higher value on the blocks than its partners did," said Leonard, adding that the partners each have options to acquire one-third interests in those blocks.
